newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dollar eases in Europe after hitting 120 yen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dollar eases in Europe after hitting 120 yen.

text.p: The dollar sank back against the yen by midsession on Friday after making a long-awaited stab at 120 yen earlier but many traders saw it as merely a correction before the bullish dollar reached for higher levels.

After poking above 120 yen for the first time in nearly four years, the dollar was driven down by talk of Bank of Japan intervention and consternation over contradictory comments about the yen by senior Japanese government officials.

"We're seeing quite an adjustment in the dollar this morning, but I'd say it was purely a healthy correction. In the longer term, the dollar still has room to rise further," said one dealer at a U.S. bank in London.
The dollar dropped to 118.80 yen by Europe's midday after hitting a high of 120.15 yen, falling below Thursday's late European level of 119.57.

Although the dollar was not expected to make further headway against the yen on Friday, analysts said economic fundamentals were all pointing towards dollar strength and that it would need more than rhetoric from Japanese officials to turn it around.

"Something that would really affect dollar/yen would be some really strong data out of Japan or some weak data out of the U.S. That would be a fundamental cause for a turnaround," said IBJ International senior analyst Roger Francis.
"But it looks like it's going to be very difficult to break the declining impetus of the yen. All the signals coming through are saying the Japanese economy is very weak," Francis said.

The market got plenty of rhetoric from Japan earlier, and traders and analysts said the fact that several officials came out to express worries about yen weakness immediately after the dollar hit 120 yen showed how concerned Tokyo was about the currency's speedy decline.
The dollar's rise earlier was sparked by a comment from Japan's Economic Planning Agency that the weak yen was not having a big negative impact on the economy.

But when the dollar hit 120 yen, a Finance Ministry official said Tokyo would not welcome an excessively weak yen and Japan's chief government spokesman said he was confident the yen would not drop below the 120-yen level.
"Japanese officials have made lots of comments about excessive yen weakness, but they've never actually said what that meant," said Lehman Brothers foreign exchange economist Francis Breedon.

"But now that they've mentioned the 120-yen figure, they will try very hard to protect it. It would be unfortunate for them if the yen went very far beyond that level, because that would reflect on their credibility," Breedon said.
But comments from Tokyo were seen as insufficient.

"What people really care about are things like their delaying the Tankan for a month, which everyone interpreted as a sign that the economy is so weak they didn't dare release it ahead of year-end for fear of crippling everyone's balance sheets when the stock market drops," IBJ's Francis said.
The Bank of Japan delayed its next Tankan report, a key quarterly survey of business sentiment, until April. Japan's business year ends on March 31.
Hard-hitting words or action from the U.S. would be needed to turn the dollar/yen market around, analysts said, although they added this was unlikely.

An opportunity for this could arise during U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's speech at an awards ceremony in Washington D.C. at 1800 GMT on Friday but most doubted anything decisive will emerge from this event.
